A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same teacher-student regression work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable: Appendices A–F in v1 and A–J in v2. Internal caption inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: Figures 1–4 report original numerical simulations of learning dynamics, generalization error, bias–variance decomposition, and regularization effects, compared with theoretical predictions.

after.justification: v2 retains simulation results and adds experiments on sample-size scaling, optimal stopping versus temperature, and static label noise, including Appendix H, Figure 6.

M1.justification: The central linear regression model, Langevin training, and variational Gaussian framework remain. Appendix H extends the effective dynamics to static label noise. Appendix J formulates a nonlinear teacher-student model and its gradient dynamics, but leaves the disorder-averaged solution for future work.

E1.justification: Appendix H and Figure 6 add an evaluated scenario with Gaussian noise on training labels, beyond v1's noiseless teacher. The synthetic Gaussian-feature regression domain remains; the nonlinear committee-machine extension is not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: Both versions compare theoretical predictions with direct simulations of the Langevin-trained model. v2's added scaling curves are predictions from its own approximations, and the Canatar comparison is an algebraic stationary-limit calculation. No additional competing method is experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: New scaling experiments use N = 1000, P = 50–300, and dt = 0.005, and Figure 5 measures stopping-time minima across temperatures. In retained experiments, plotted legends add β = 1 and replace gβ = 1 with 0.5. These extend settings within the existing simulation framework.

E4.justification: New Figures 4–5 test asymptotic bias/variance scaling, finite-size corrections, and the temperature dependence of optimal stopping. Appendix H and Figure 6 additionally analyze sensitivity to static label noise. These substantially extend v1's analyses of dynamic noise and regularization.

E5.justification: Retained experiments still report averaging over 10^5 training-data realizations. New Figures 4 and 5 specify 10^2 and 5 × 10^3 realizations, respectively. These are additional experiment-specific replication counts, not evidence that retained experiments received more runs. No confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v2 adds sample-size-dependent loss curves and minima, an approximately linear stopping-time-versus-β trend, and label-noise results showing earlier, higher-error minima with stronger noise. Retained plots also add β = 1 and replace the gβ = 1 result with 0.5. These are additional or differently configured results, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G add explicit bias/variance scaling laws, finite-size corrections, and t* = βα/[2(1+α)]. Appendices B–C add arguments concerning concentration and Gaussian exactness. New Appendices H–J derive label-noise dynamics, a stationary-limit connection, and a nonlinear model formulation. These substantially expand the mathematical substance.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction's contribution list remain essentially unchanged. The discussion now makes the stopping-time dependence and minimum-loss scaling explicit, claims recovery of the stationary result, and adds label-noise applicability and an outlined nonlinear extension.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G add substantive interpretations of the sample-size/noise tradeoff and finite-size corrections. They identify conditions for the new scaling approximation, including α > 0, weak regularization, and dominant thermal noise, and explain why its stationary limit cannot generally be taken. v1 lacked this analysis of scaling behavior and applicability.

D1.justification: Captions provide configurations and integration steps for the added experiments, and the acknowledgements newly identify JURECA computing resources. Neither PDF supplies a code repository or a detailed reproduction workflow.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning within static and dynamic scaling-law research, adding discussions of Bordelon–Canatar–Pehlevan, Cui, Spigler, Defilippis, Atanasov, and Paquette and collaborators. It explicitly distinguishes identical teacher/student features and Langevin dynamics from down-projected models and finite-batch SGD. Appendix I adds a detailed connection to Canatar's stationary theory.

P1.justification: Related work is reorganized into static and dynamic approaches, several passages are edited, and appendix explanations are expanded. A scaling-law section precedes the discussion. Most existing prose and derivations remain closely matched; the substantial scientific additions do not constitute a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 2–3 are combined and redrawn as v2 Figure 2, with changed legends and plotting ranges. The regularization panels are reordered and relabeled. New Figures 4–6 add scaling curves, a minimum-loss inset, stopping-time points, and label-noise curves, substantially expanding the visual evidence.

improvement.justification: v1 promises analytical scaling and optimal-stopping results but mainly supplies dynamical equations and illustrative learning curves. v2 supplies explicit predictions, derivations, and targeted simulations in Section 5, Appendix G, and Figures 4–5, addressing an important gap in the central contribution. The tested label-noise extension adds further substance. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies, including Figure 2's outdated caption and Appendix I's final stationary-loss formula dropping the factor 1/2 present in Equations 79–80.
